findings.title: Arrival at a boundary becomes a limit on communication
findings.claim: In 18:93, arrival between the barriers is also presented as reaching a communicative limit: the people can be encountered while scarcely taking in speech, yet the later exchange leaves coordination open.
findings.mechanism: The completed arrival carried by بَلَغَ meets the speech-content and failed-comprehension clause carried by قَوْلًا and its surrounding predicate; the supplied same-surah and inter-ayah relations extend that contact to purposeful travel, defined boundaries, and difficulty receiving speech.
findings.reader_payoff: The scene becomes more than a destination and an unfamiliar people: contact reaches the edge of shared intelligibility without making action impossible.
findings.containment: The packet supports a communicative limit and continued coordination. It does not determine whether the exchange was direct, translated, gestural, or otherwise mediated, and it does not turn this local relation into a surah thesis.

epistemic.reason: A trusted cross-run publication supplies the exact focus anchors and the bounded relation between physical boundary, speech difficulty, and later coordination; the legacy reader-walk inference is not required for this finding.

findings.title: Shared speech remains sufficient for practical coordination
findings.claim: The focus presents speech as severely difficult to understand, while the ensuing exchange shows that this difficulty still leaves room for a proposal, response, and coordinated work.
findings.mechanism: بَلَغَ and قَوْلًا bring arrival and speech into one contact; the supplied 18:94-96 continuation changes that contact from apparent communicative blockage into a bounded, negotiated form of cooperation.
findings.reader_payoff: Limited intelligibility becomes friction that practical action can traverse, so coordination appears through negotiated work rather than eloquence alone.
findings.containment: The near-failure of comprehension remains intact. The packet does not decide whether the exchange used translation, gesture, partial speech, or another mediation, and it does not establish a general governance thesis.

epistemic.reason: The reader-walk and retrospective support explicitly infer the transition from speech friction to coordinated action, but the later continuation is not supplied with a complete word-level anchor trace in this lane packet.

findings.title: The two barriers and blocked understanding share an obstruction pattern
findings.claim: The two barriers can be heard as a physical obstruction whose image meets the community's inability to take in speech, so the scene contains two forms of blocked passage: terrain closes space and impairment closes reception.
findings.mechanism: ٱلسَّدَّيْنِ supplies the paired physical barrier; the speech-comprehension clause supplies an independent communicative trigger, activating the barrier facet and the s-d-d impairment facet at the same focus carrier.
findings.reader_payoff: The setting and the people's difficulty illuminate each other: the verse makes a physical enclosure and a failure of reception perceptible together.
findings.containment: This is a bounded lexical resonance, not a claim that the barriers are themselves a bodily speech defect and not a replacement of the primary geography. The possible intentionality of the mirror remains open.

epistemic.reason: The trusted publication anchors both focus branches, but its own relation is recorded as weak retrieval evidence and the impairment branch is marked reframed; the mirror is therefore retained with its boundary visible.

findings.reader_payoff: The barrier scene becomes a model of constrained agency whose answer is coordinated material work, while the initial difficulty remains visible.
findings.containment: The packet supports this as an attributed reader-walk resonance. It does not establish an exclusive authorial design, a universal governance theory, or a single communication mode.
